verses.zh: 我将这一切事放在心上，详细考究，就知道义人和智慧人，并他们的作为都在　神手中；或是爱，或是恨，都在他们的前面，人不能知道。
verses.en: So I reflected on all this,[NOTE:1] attempting to clear[NOTE:2] it all up.I concluded that[NOTE:3] the righteous and the wise, as well as their works, are in the hand of God;whether a person will be loved or hated[NOTE:4]—no one knows what lies ahead.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “I laid all this to my heart.”

The term וְלָבוּר (velavur, conjunction plus Qal infinitive construct from בּוּר, bur, “to make clear”) denotes “to examine; to make clear; to clear up; to explain” (HALOT 116 s.v. בור; BDB 101 s.v. בּוּר). The term is related to Arabic baraw “to examine” (G. R. Driver, “Supposed Arabisms in the Old Testament,” JBL 55 [1936]: 108). This verb is related to the Hebrew noun בֹּר (bor, “cleanness”) and adjective בַּר (bar, “clean”). The term is used in the OT only in Ecclesiastes (1:13; 2:3; 7:25; 9:1). This use of the infinitive has a connotative sense (“attempting to”), and functions in a complementary sense, relative to the main verb.
The words “I concluded that” do not appear in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “whether love or hatred.”
Heb “man does not know anything before them.”
verses.commentary:
9:1

NASB
"For I have taken all this to my heart and explain. . ."

NKJV
"For I considered all this in my heart so that I could declare it all:"

NRSV
"All this I laid to heart, examining it all"

REB
"To all this I applied my mind, and I understood‒"

NJB
"Yes, I have applied myself to all this and experienced all this to be so:"

TEV
"I thought long and hard about all this"

NET
"So I reflected on all this, attempting to clear it all up"

JPSOA
"For all this I noted, and I ascertained all this:"

This sounds very much like chapters 1 and 2 (Solomon as literary foil). The author's mind and experience led him
to affirm that life is unknowable and unfair.

There is a textual issue at the beginning of v. 1.

- "I took to heart"

- "I set my heart"

The UBS Text Project suggests option 1, which is followed by RSV, NEB.

▣ Notice the parallelism:

- righteous men (BDB 843)

- wise men (BDB 314)

Wise persons are righteous persons (cf. Prov. 1:13; 9:9; 23:24). The righteous
and the wicked are contrasted in Eccl. 9:2:

- the righteous vs. the wicked

- the good vs. the bad (LXX)

- the clean vs. the unclean

- the man who offers a sacrifice vs. the one who does not

- the man who does not swear vs. the one who takes oaths lightly

The "wicked" and "righteous" both refer to covenant people (not Gentiles). This
follows the theology of Deut. 31:29 and Jdg. 2:19.

NASB
"explain"

NKJV
"declare"

NRSV
"examine"

NJB
"experienced"

LXX
"has seen"

REB
"understood"

JPSOA
"ascertained"

Peshitta
"considered"

This word (BDB 101, KB 116, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
means "to make clear" or "explain" (from the Arabic root, "to examine"). There
is some question about the text at this point and some scholars

- assume that the VERB is a misprint for "seek out"
(BDB 1064, KB 1707), found at Eccl. 1:13; 2:3; 7:25, where the initial t
and b are confused

- believe that the INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT comes from brr
(BDB 140, KB 162), meaning "to be clear" or "to select." It is used in Eccl. 3:18
in the sense of "test" or "purify" (cf. Ps. 18:26)

- divide the Hebrew consonants differently (cf. LXX, "seen")

▣ "deeds" This is the only place in the OT where this word (BDB 714), which normally
is a VERBAL used of "service to God," is used as a NOUN.

▣ "their deeds are in the hand of God" This is the continuing theme of God's sovereignty
("hand" equals "power," cf. Eccl. 2:24; Job 19:21; 27:11; Ps. 10:12; 17:7; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND) and humanity's ignorance
of the cause or reason of present events and future events! Fallen humans do not control anything
but still have life choices with consequences!

Scripture assures believers that their lives are in the hand (i.e., control) of
God (e.g., Deut. 33:3; Job 12:10; Ps. 119:109; Matt. 6:25-34). However, experience teaches that
bad things happen to good people. Life is uncertain at best, yet God is sure and faithful. Faith
sees through life's uncertainties and beholds God! Life is uncertain and undependable, but God is certain
and dependable! Maybe life is a test to see who really trusts God!

For "hand" see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "Man does not know whether it will be love or hatred, anything awaits him" Life
is unpredictable and uncontrollable (contra idolatry, cf. Deuteronomy 18), even for those who serve God
(cf. Eccl. 9:2,11; 3:22; 6:12; 7:14; 8:7; 10:14). This is the agnostic philosophy that bothered the later rabbis.
It totally challenges the "two ways" of traditional wisdom.

The JPSOA sugests an emendation, "even love, even hate, no man can know in advance.
All are insignificant." The events of life may be insignificant in the big picture of human history, but they are significant to

- the individual and his/her family

- the God of creation who has an eternal plan

verses.zh: 凡临到众人的事都是一样：义人和恶人都遭遇一样的事；好人，洁净人和不洁净人，献祭的与不献祭的，也是一样。好人如何，罪人也如何；起誓的如何，怕起誓的也如何。
verses.en: Everyone shares the same fate[NOTE:1]—the righteous and the wicked,the good and the bad,[NOTE:2] the ceremonially clean and unclean,those who offer sacrifices and those who do not.What happens to the good person, also happens to the sinner;[NOTE:3] what happens to those who make vows, also happens to those who are afraid to make vows.
notes: Heb “all things just as to everyone, one fate.”

The MT reads simply “the good,” but the Greek versions read “the good and the bad.” In contrast to the other four pairs in v. 2 (“the righteous and the wicked,” “those who sacrifice, and those who do not sacrifice,” “the good man…the sinner,” and “those who make vows…those who are afraid to make vows”), the MT has a triad in the second line: לַטּוֹב וְלַטָּהוֹר וְלַטָּמֵא (lattov velattahor velattameʾ, “the good, and the clean, and the unclean”). This reading in the Leningrad Codex (ca. a.d. 1008)—the basis of the BHS and BHK publications of the MT—is also supported by the Ben Asher text of the First Rabbinic Bible (“the Soncino Bible”) published in a.d. 1488-94. On the other hand, the Greek version in B (Aquila) has two pairs: “the good and the bad, and the clean and the unclean.” Either Aquila inserted καὶ τῷ κακῷ (kai tō kakō, “and the bad”) to fill out a pair and to create six parallel pairs in v. 2, or Aquila reflects an early Hebrew textual tradition tradition of לַטּוֹב וְלַרָע (lattov velaraʿ, “the good and the bad”). Since Aquila is well known for his commitment to a literal—at times even a mechanically wooden—translation of the Hebrew, with no room for improvisation, it is more than likely that Aquila is reflecting an authentic Hebrew textual tradition. Aquila dates to a.d. 130, while the Leningrad Codex dates to a.d. 1008; therefore, the Vorlage of Aquila might have been the original Hebrew textual tradition, being much earlier than the MT of the Leningrad Codex. The alternate textual tradition of Aquila is also seen in the Syriac and Latin versions (but these are dependent upon the Greek = Aquila). On the other hand, the editors of BHK and BHS suggest that the presence of the anomalous לַטּוֹב was an addition to the Hebrew text, and should be deleted. They also suggest that the Greek pair τῷ ἀγαθῷ καὶ τῷ κακῷ (tō agathō kai tō kakō, “the good and the bad”) does not reflect an alternate textual tradition, but that their Vorlage contained only לַטּוֹב: the Greek version intentionally added καὶ τῷ κακῷ (kai tō kakō, “and the bad”) to create a pair. The English versions are divided. Several follow the Greek: “the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean” (NEB, NAB, RSV, NRSV, NIV, Moffatt, NLT). Others follow the Hebrew: “the good and the clean and the unclean” (KJV, ASV, MLB, NJPS). None, however, delete “the good” (לַטּוֹב) as suggested by the BHK and BHS editors. If the shorter text were original, the addition of καὶ τῷ κακῷ would be intentional. If the longer text were original, the omission of וְלַרָע (“and the bad”) could have caused by unintentional homoioarcton (“similar beginning”) in the three-fold repetition of לט in לַטּוֹב וְלַרָע וְלַטָּהוֹר וְלַטָּמֵא (lattov velaraʿ velattahor velattameʾ, “the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean”). The term וְלַרָע (“and the bad”) was accidentally omitted when a scribe skipped from the first occurrence of לט in לַטּוֹב to its second occurrence in the word וְלַטָּהוֹר (“the clean”).
Heb “As is the good (man), so is the sinner.”
verses.commentary:
9:2 "It is the same for all" The same events (i.e., death) occur in the life of the wicked and
the righteous (cf. Eccl. 9:3,11; 2:14-15; 3:19-20). If the promises of God are sure, how can this be
true? This is the mystery of this fallen age (i.e., the uncertainty of life, but the certainty of
death [cf. Rom. 5:12,17,18-19])! True life is more than a physical, earthly experience!

Notice the contrasting pairs used to make the point.

- the righteous ‒ the wicked

- the clean ‒ the unclean (i.e., ritual purity)

- thosel who sacrifice ‒ those who do not (i.e., Eccl. 5:1)

- good man ‒ sinner (i.e., Eccl. 2:26; 7:26)

- swearer ‒ those who do not swear/vow (i.e., Eccl. 8:2)

The summary is in v. 3, "there is one fate for all men"—death.

The MT, after #1, has "to the good," but does not finish the suggested contrast. The LXX adds
"and the bad." If so, then there are six contrasting pairs.

verses.zh: 在日光之下所行的一切事上有一件祸患，就是众人所遭遇的都是一样，并且世人的心充满了恶；活着的时候心里狂妄，后来就归死人那里去了。
verses.en: This is the unfortunate fact[NOTE:1] about everything that happens on earth:[NOTE:2] The same fate awaits[NOTE:3] everyone.In addition to this, the hearts of all people[NOTE:4] are full of evil,and there is folly in their hearts during their lives—then they die.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “evil.”
Heb “under the sun.”
The term “awaits” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for smoothness and stylistic reasons.
Heb “also the heart of the sons of man.” Here “heart” is a collective singular.
Heb “and after that [they go] to [the place of] the dead.”
verses.commentary:
9:3 "in all that is done under the sun" This is a major interpretive theme (see full note
at Eccl. 1:3). It is used six times in this chapter. It denotes the consequences of earthly life without God.

▣ "one fate for all men" This is a reaction to the traditional OT theology that asserts that
if you love and obey God, He will prosper you physically and spiritually (i.e., Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-30).
It is often called "the two ways" (cf. Ps. 1). The book of Job and Psalm 73 also react against the
imbalance of this performance-based worldview when compared to experience (cf. Eccl. 3:19-20).

▣ "the hearts of the sons of men are full of evil" This is the result of the Fall of mankind
recorded in Genesis 3, illustrated in Genesis 4, and stated specifically in Gen. 6:5,11-12,13; 8:21; Ps. 14:3;
58:3; notice Rom. 3:10-18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

NASB
"insanity"

NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, REB, LXX
"madness"

NJB
"folly"

Peshitta
"grievous error"

This word (BDB 239, KB 242) is used only in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 1:17; 2:12; 7:25; 9:3; and
a related form in Eccl. 10:13). It seems to be related to the word for "praise" (same three CONSONANTS but
different VOWELS).

Possibly similar to

- Saul's experience in 1 Sam. 10:6,10-11

- David's in 1 Sam. 21:14 (BDB 237 II)

In Eccl. 1:17 and 2:12 the meaning is parallel to a search for wisdom and does not have
a negative connotation. However, in Eccl. 7:25 and 9:3 it is parallel with "evil" and is obviously
negative. The first pair describes the author's search for meaning and a lasting advantage, but the
last pair describes fallen humanity (cf. Gen. 6:5,11-12,13; 8:21; Rom. 3:9-18). The real theological question is, "Does
Qoheleth's thought focus

- on Genesis 3 (i.e., sin, cf. Rom. 3:10-31)

- on covenant obedience (i.e., Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:1,15,19)?

verses.zh: 与一切活人相连的，那人还有指望，因为活着的狗比死了的狮子更强。
verses.en: But whoever is among[NOTE:1] the living[NOTE:2] has hope;a live dog is better than a dead lion.
notes: The consonantal text (Kethib) has “is chosen, selected.” The translation follows the marginal reading (Qere), “is joined.” See BDB 288 s.v. חָבַר Pu.
Heb “all the living.”
verses.commentary:
9:4 Life is better than death because there still remains the chance to know God (i.e., "there
is hope," BDB 105, KB 120 I, lit. "trust," cf. 2 Kgs. 18:19). It is difficult to know when Qoheleth is using
sarcasm versus tongue-in-cheek wisdom sayings. At points he seems to contradict himself. At these
points several exact opposite interpretations are possible! Is he

- totally pessimistic (i.e., "there is no hope)

- pessimistic with glimpses of hope here and there (i.e., there is possible hope)

- always speaking sarcastically about the fallen world (i.e., there is always hope with God)?

It seems best to me to choose #2. This interpretive stance allows for "under the sun"
(see notes at Eccl. 1:3) sarcasm, but also allows hope texts (i.e., Eccl. 8:2:2-26; 3:12,13,22;
5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).

The MT has the VERB "chosen" (BDB 103,
KB 119, Pual IMPERFECT), but the Masoretic scholars
recognized this should read "joined" (Qere, BDB 287, KB 287,
LXX, Peshitta), which reverses the first two consonants.

▣ "dog" They were street scavengers (BDB 476) not pets (i.e., Ps. 59:6,14; 1 Kgs. 14:11).

▣ "lion" The predominant beast of prey in this geography. See
SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

verses.zh: 活着的人知道必死；死了的人毫无所知，也不再得赏赐；他们的名无人记念。
verses.en: For the living know that they will die, but the dead do not know anything;they have no further reward—and even the memory of them disappears.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “for their memory is forgotten.” The pronominal suffix is an objective genitive, “memory of them.”
verses.commentary:
9:5-6 The "under the sun" logic (sarcasm) of Qoheleth drives him to search for a lasting
advantage/profit (see note at Eccl. 1:3). If there is no God, there is no lasting advantage:

- the living struggle with the fear of death ("know," BDB 393, KB 562,
Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)

- the living seek happiness ("reward," BDB 969 I)

- the living seek memorials ("no memory," BDB 271), but in the end the life experience of
all humans is the same

- death (cf. Eccl. 9:2,3,6,11; 3:20)

- there is no lasting advantage

- no share (i.e., reward, cf. Eccl. 9:6 [BDB 324]) in life!

He comes to this conclusion based on life observances. This is an unfair, unjust, and
surprisingly evil world. Often the promises of God seem not to be fulfilled in this life! The wicked
prosper and have longevity! What can a godly person do? The book as a whole gives two answers:

- enjoy life when and where you can (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9)

- trust God and keep the commandments (even if the lasting advantage is not apparent, cf. Eccl. 12:13-14)

9:5 "for their memory is forgotten" This concept of memory/remembrance is viewed in several ways.

- the wicked pagan nations and their leaders/people will not be remembered (Ps. 9:5-6; Exod. 17:14; Deut. 25:19; 32:26; Isa. 26:14)

- the righteous will be remembered (Ps. 112:6; Prov. 10:7)

- the wicked among the covenant people will not be remembered (Eccl. 8:10; Ps. 34:16; 69:28; 109:13,15)

- Qoheleth's reaction to traditonal wisdom, even the righteous will not be remembered (Eccl. 2:16; 9:5)

- all memory of human activity will be forgotten (Eccl. 1:11; 2:16; 9:5)

verses.zh: 他们的爱，他们的恨，他们的嫉妒，早都消灭了。在日光之下所行的一切事上，他们永不再有分了。
verses.en: What they loved,[NOTE:1] as well as what they hated[NOTE:2] and envied,[NOTE:3] perished long ago,and they no longer have a part in anything that happens on earth.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “their love.”
Heb “their hatred.”
Heb “their envy.”
Heb “under the sun.”
verses.commentary:
9:6 This verse describes the fleeting, transitory life of humans. The term "share"
(BDB 324, KB 324) is translated

- "reward" in Eccl. 2:10; 5:18,19; 9:9

- "lot" in Eccl. 3:22

- "portion" in Eccl. 11:2

It is the term used for God's allotment of land to the tribes in Deuteronomy and Joshua.

verses.zh: 你只管去欢欢喜喜吃你的饭，心中快乐喝你的酒，因为　神已经悦纳你的作为。
verses.en: Go, eat your food[NOTE:1] with joy,and drink your wine with a happy heart,because God has already approved your works.
notes: Heb “your bread.”
verses.commentary:
9:7-9 This is Qoheleth's answer to the futility and uncertainty of human existence! Notice
all the commands:

- "go," Eccl. 9:7, BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "eat," Eccl. 9:7, BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Eccl. 2:24;
3:13; 5:18; 8:15

- "drink," Eccl. 9:7, BDB 1059, KB 1667, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf.
Eccl. 2:24; 3:13; 5:18; 8:15; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

- "let your clothes be white all the time," Eccl. 9:8, BDB 224, KB 243, Qal
IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "let not oil be lacking on your head," Eccl. 9:8, BDB 341, KB 338,
Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "enjoy life with the woman. . .," Eccl. 9:9, BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal
IMPERATIVE, lit. "see" (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SEXUALITY)

- "do it with all your might," Eccl. 9:10, BDB 793, KB 889, Qal
IMPERATIVE, cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:13,22; 5:18; 8:15

Happiness is found not in wisdom, pleasure, or possessions, but in the simple pleasures
of daily life.

- home, family

- work

- friends

- contentment with gratitude to God for what you have, not what you do not have

Life is a journey, not a destination! Smell the roses, kiss your wife and kids, go to work with joy!

These verses are very similar to the Epic of Gilgamesh (Babylonian Wisdom Literature)
10.3.6-14. This is a good illustration of the transcultural nature of ANE Wisdom Literature.

9:7 "drink your wine with a cheerful heart" See

BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

NASB, NJB, LXX
"for God has already approved your works"

NKJV
"for God has already accepted your works"

NRSV
"for God has long ago approved what you do"

TEV
"It's all right with God"

JPSOA
"for your action was long ago approved by God"

REB
"for God already accepted what you have done"

Peshitta
"for God is pleased with your works"

This cannot refer to sin and rebellion, so it must refer to God's activity within
this fallen world (see Eccl. 2:24; 3:13; 5:19; 8:15)! Life is hard, but we are not alone! God has
approved those who trust Him. In this context it refers to "eating" and "drinking," which could refer
to a daily activity or a religious or social festival (cf. Eccl. 9:8; 8:15).

verses.zh: 你的衣服当时常洁白，你头上也不要缺少膏油。
verses.en: Let your clothes always be white,and do not spare precious ointment on your head.
verses.commentary:
9:8 "Let your clothes be white" We cannot control circumstances, but we can control our reaction
to them. Those who trust God have a positive mind set, which is not affected by circumstances
(see Hannah Whithall Smith's The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life).

▣ "oil" Putting oil on the face and arms was

- a sign of gladness (cf. Ps. 23:5; 45:7; 104:15; Isa. 61:3)

- preparation for social events

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

verses.zh: 在你一生虚空的年日，就是　神赐你在日光之下虚空的年日，当同你所爱的妻，快活度日，因为那是你生前在日光之下劳碌的事上所得的分。
verses.en: Enjoy[NOTE:1] life with your beloved wife[NOTE:2] during all the days of your fleeting[NOTE:3] lifethat God[NOTE:4] has given you on earth[NOTE:5] during all your fleeting days;[NOTE:6] for that is your reward in life and in your burdensome work[NOTE:7] on earth.[NOTE:8]
notes: Heb “see.”
Heb “the wife whom you love.”

As discussed in the note on the word “futile” in 1:2, the term הֶבֶל (hevel) has a wide range of meanings, and should not be translated the same in every place (see HALOT 236-37 s.v. I הֶבֶל; BDB 210-11 s.v. I הבֶל). The term is used in two basic ways in OT, literally and figuratively. The literal, concrete sense is used in reference to the wind, man’s transitory breath, evanescent vapor (Isa 57:13; Pss 62:10; 144:4; Prov 21:6; Job 7:16). In this sense, it is often a synonym for “breath; wind” (Eccl 1:14; Isa 57:13; Jer 10:14). The literal sense lent itself to the metaphorical sense. Because breath/vapor/wind is transitory and fleeting, the figurative connotation “fleeting; transitory” arose (e.g., Prov 31:30; Eccl 6:12; 7:15; 9:9; 11:10; Job 7:16). In this sense, it is parallel to “few days” and “[days] which he passes like a shadow” (Eccl 6:12). It is used in reference to youth and vigor (11:10) or life (6:12; 7:15; 9:9) which are “transitory” or “fleeting.” In this context, the most appropriate meaning is “fleeting.”
Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “under the sun”

The phrase כָּל יְמֵי הֶבְלֶךָ (kol yeme hevlekha, “all your fleeting days”) is present in the MT, but absent in the Greek versions, other medieval Hebrew mss, and the Targum. Its appearance in the MT may be due to dittography (repetition: the scribe wrote twice what should have been written once) from כָּל יְמֵי חַיֵּי הֶבְלֶךָ (kol yeme khayye hevlekha, “all the days of your fleeting life”) which appears in the preceding line. On the other hand, its omission in the alternate textual tradition may be due to haplography (accidental omission of repeated words) with the earlier line.
Heb “in your toil in which you toil.”
Heb “under the sun.”
verses.commentary:
9:9 "Enjoy life with the woman you love all the days of your fleeting life" This
command ("enjoy" Qal IMPERATIVE) implies
monogamy ("love," BDB 12, KB 17, Qal PERFECT, cf. Prov. 5:18-19).
Marital contentment is a great blessing from God.

The question remains, does "woman" (BDB 61),
without the ARTICLE, refer to "wife" or "woman?" The problem is
Qoheleth's seemingly negative view of women found in Eccl. 7:26 and 28. Does this verse encourage
monogamous marriage (if so the author cannot be Solomon!)? The Qal
PERFECT VERB "love" implies a complete union, not brief encounters!

Wisdom Literature used "woman" in two ways:

- wife to be loved, protected, and kept

- woman as temptress and symbol of false wisdom or momentary pleasure

As Wisdom Literature used both senses, so too, does Qoheleth!

▣ "your fleeting life" This is the Hebrew NOUN ה (hebel). It was the
name of Adam and Eve's second son, Abel (BDB 211 II). It is often used of the breath of humans. Its major usage is
as imagery of transitoriness (cf. Eccl. 6:12; 7:15; 9:9; 11:10). In this context it encourages wise humans to enjoy their family life.

This is the same root that occurs in Eccl. 1:2. It is a major theological concept in Ecclesiastes. See full nte at Eccl. 1:2.

▣ "in your toil in which you have labored" The Hebrew root עמל (labor, toil, BDB 765, 766 II) denotes
man's labor to support his family (cf. Eccl. 2:10,20,21,22,24; 3:13; 4:4,6,8,9; 5:18; 10:15). It implies hard work.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SEXUALITY

verses.zh: 凡你手所当做的事要尽力去做；因为在你所必去的阴间没有工作，没有谋算，没有知识，也没有智慧。
verses.en: Whatever you find to do with your hands,[NOTE:1] do it with all your might,because there is neither work nor planning nor knowledge nor wisdom in the grave,[NOTE:2] the place where you will eventually go.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Whatever your hand finds to do.”
Heb “Sheol.”
Or “where you are about to go.”
verses.commentary:
9:10 "Whatever your hand finds to do, verily do it with all your might" See note at
Eccl. 9:7-9, #7. Physical labor originally was not a consequence of sin, but part of Adam's
God-given task in the Garden of Eden (cf. Gen. 2:15). After the Fall labor became a curse
(cf. Gen. 3:19). In this context labor refers to making a daily living (i.e., food, shelter,
home, family, etc). This aspect of life is a gift from God. It takes our minds off the task
of trying to discover God and His purposes, which we cannot do. Work is good! From the NT
perspective it can glorify God (cf. Eccl. 11:6; John 9:4; Col. 3:17,23; Eph. 6:5-7). Do all you
do as unto the Lord Jesus!

SPECIAL TOPIC: GARDEN OF EDEN

▣ "there is no activity or planning or wisdom in Sheol where you are going" The OT
(except for Job 14:14-15; 19:25-27; Ps. 16:9-10; 49:15; 86:13) depicts death as a conscious but
shadowy existence. The faithful are with their families, but there is no fellowship, joy, or activity.
Death is a place or abode, but nothing more (e.g., 1:11; 9:5; Job 3:13-19; 10:21-22). Thank God for
the progressive revelation of the New Testament!

Notice the things that humans do not do in Sheol:

- activity ("work," BDB 795, cf. Eccl. 2:4,11; 3:17,22; 8:9; 9:7,10)

- planning (or "reckoning schemes," BDB 363 I, cf. Eccl. 7:25,27)

- pursue knowledge (BDB 395, cf. Eccl. 1:16,18; 2:21,26; 7:12)

- gain wisdom (BDB 315, cf. Eccl. 1:13,16 [twice], 18; 2:3,9,13,21; 7:10,11,12 [twice],
19,23; 8:1; 9:10, 15,16 [twice], 18; 10:1,10)

verses.zh: 我又转念：见日光之下，快跑的未必能赢；力战的未必得胜；智慧的未必得粮食；明哲的未必得资财；灵巧的未必得喜悦。所临到众人的是在乎当时的机会。
verses.en: Again,[NOTE:1] I observed this on the earth:[NOTE:2] The race is not always[NOTE:3] won by the swiftest,the battle is not always won by the strongest;prosperity[NOTE:4] does not always belong to those who are the wisest;wealth does not always belong to those who are the most discerning,nor does success[NOTE:5] always come to those with the most knowledge—for time and chance may overcome[NOTE:6] them all.
notes: Heb “I returned and.” In the Hebrew idiom, “to return and do” means “to do again.”
Heb “under the sun.”
The term “always” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation (five times in this verse) for clarity.
Heb “bread.”
Heb “favor.”
Heb “happen to.”
verses.commentary:
9:11-12 These verses highlight the ineffectualness and helplessness of human effort! They again
magnify the sovereignty of God. This conclusion is based on the unfairness and injustice that Qoheleth
had seen and experienced. Life is unpredictable and uncontrollable (i.e., "for time and chance
overtake them all," cf. Eccl. 9:12; 8:7).

His conclusions to this situations are

- enjoy life when and where you can; death is coming

- trust God even if He is unknown and invisible

- there is an afterlife and humans will give an account of the gifts and stewardship of life (cf. Matt. 25:31-46;
Rom. 14:10-12; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 20:11-14)

As I sit here writing this, I am so glad I live in a post-resurrection era. Progressive
revelation, the life of Jesus, the gospel, the empty tomb are ours! New Testament believers understand
so much more of the eternal plans and purposes of God than any OT person.
The real question for us is, "What are we doing with this information?"!

verses.zh: 原来人也不知道自己的定期。鱼被恶网圈住，鸟被网罗捉住，祸患忽然临到的时候，世人陷在其中也是如此。
verses.en: Surely, no one[NOTE:1] knows his appointed time.[NOTE:2] Like fish that are caught in a deadly[NOTE:3] net and like birds that are caught in a snare—just like them, all people[NOTE:4] are ensnared[NOTE:5] at an unfortunate[NOTE:6] time that falls upon them suddenly.
notes: Heb “man.” The term is used here in a generic sense and translated “no one.”

Heb “time.” BDB 773 s.v. עֵת 2.d suggests that עֵת (ʿet, “time”) refers to an “uncertain time.” On the other hand, HALOT 901 s.v. עֵת 6 nuances it as “destined time,” that is, “no one knows his destined time [i.e., hour of destiny].” It is used in parallelism with זְמָן (zeman, “appointed time; appointed hour”) in 3:1 (HALOT 273 s.v. זְמָן; BDB 273 s.v. זְמָן). Eccl 3:9-15 teaches God’s sovereignty over the appointed time-table of human events. Similarly, Qoheleth here notes that no one knows what God has appointed in any situation or time. This highlights the limitations of human wisdom and human ability, as 9:11 stresses.
Heb “bad, evil.” The moral connotation hardly fits here. The adjective would seem to indicate that the net is the instrument whereby the fish come to ruin.
Heb “the sons of man.”

The Masoretes pointed the consonantal form יוקשׁים (“are ensnared”) as יוּקָשִׁים (yuqashim, Pual participle mpl from יָקֹשׁ , yaqosh, “to be ensnared”). This is an unusual form for a Pual participle: (1) The characteristic doubling of the middle consonant was omitted due to the lengthening of the preceding short vowel from יֻקָּשִׁים to יוּקָשִׁים (GKC 74 §20.n and 143 §52.s), and (2) The characteristic prefix מ (mem) is absent, as in a few other Pual participles, e.g., Exod 3:2; Judg 13:8; 2 Kgs 2:10; Isa 30:24; 54:11 (GKC 143 §52.s). On the other hand, the consonant form יוקשים might actually be an example of the old Qal passive participle which dropped out of Hebrew at an early stage, and was frequently mistaken by the Masoretes as a Pual form (e.g., Jer 13:10; 23:32) (GKC 143 §52.s). Similarly, the Masoretes pointed אכל as אֻכָּל (ʾukkal, Pual perfect third person masculine singular “he was eaten”); however, it probably should be pointed אֻכַל (ʾukhal, old Qal passive perfect third person masculine singular “he was eaten”) because אָכַל (ʾakhal) only occurs in the Qal (see IBHS 373-74 §22.6a).

Heb “evil.” The term רָעָה (raʿah, “evil; unfortunate”) is repeated in v. 12 in the two parts of the comparison: “fish are caught in an evil (רָעָה) net” and “men are ensnared at an unfortunate (רָעָה) time.”
verses.commentary:
9:12

NASB, NJB, Peshitta
"treacherous net"

NKJV, NRSV
"cruel net"

REB
"destroying net"

JPSOA
"fatal net"

NET
"deadly net"

I show these options to illustrate how words have meaning only in sentences. The MT has the ADJECTIVE
"evil" (BDB948). This usage carries no connotation of moral evil. Here, it denotes the mechanism of the death of fish. Context, context, context!

This ADJECTIVE appears again in this verse relating to humans. Again the connotation is not "evil" but

- "unfortunate" (NET)

- "calamity" (JPSOA, NRSV)

- "misfortune" (NJB, REB)

Comparing English translations from differing translation theories often helps interpreters see the semantical
field and/or connotations of Hebrew roots.

verses.zh: 我见日光之下有一样智慧，据我看乃是广大，
verses.en: This is what I also observed about wisdom on earth,[NOTE:1] and it is a great burden[NOTE:2] to me:
notes: Heb “under the sun.”
The term “burden” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
9:13-18 This sounds like a specific historical event that Qoheleth had observed (i.e., a
series of eight Qal PERFECT VERBS; LXX makes
them SUBJUNCTIVES, implying a hypothetical situation). These
verses magnify "wisdom," but in the end it is ignored and forgotten! The wise man can affect
things, but so can the sinner (cf. Eccl. 9:18).

9:13

NASB
"it impressed me"

NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta
"it seemed great to me"

NJB
"it strikes me as important"

REB
"I find it of great significance"

JPSOA
"it affected me profoundly"

NET
"it is a great burden to me"

As Qoheleth tried to make sense of life, it was like a stimulant, but he could not figure it out. Life on this
planet, in this period, is mysterious, unpredictable, unfair, and deadly!

verses.zh: 就是有一小城，其中的人数稀少，有大君王来攻击，修筑营垒，将城围困。
verses.en: There was once[NOTE:1] a small city with a few men in it,and a mighty king attacked it, besieging[NOTE:2] it and building strong[NOTE:3] siege works against it.
notes: The verbs in this section function either as past definite actions (describing a past situation) or as hypothetical past actions (describing an imaginary hypothetical situation for the sake of illustration). The LXX uses subjunctives throughout vv. 14-15 to depict the scenario as a hypothetical situation: “Suppose there was a little city, and a few men [lived] in it; and there should come against it a great king, and surround it, and build great siege-works against it; and should find in it a poor wise man, and he should save the city through his wisdom; yet no man would remember that poor man.”

The two perfect tense verbs וְסָבַב (vesavav, “he besieged”) and וּבָנָה (uvanah, “he built”) may be taken in a complementary sense, qualifying the action of the main perfect tense verb וּבָא (uvaʾ, “he attacked it”).

The root גדל (“mighty; strong; large”) is repeated in 9:13b for emphasis: “a mighty (גָדוֹל, gadol) king…building strong (גְדֹלִים, gedolim) siege works.” This repetition highlights the contrast between the vast power and resources of the attacking king, and the meager resources of the “little” (קְטַנָּה, qetannah) city with “few” (מְעָט, meʿat) men in it to defend it.

verses.zh: 城中有一个贫穷的智慧人，他用智慧救了那城，却没有人记念那穷人。
verses.en: However, a poor but wise man lived in the city,[NOTE:1] and he could have delivered[NOTE:2] the city by his wisdom,but no one listened to[NOTE:3] that poor man.
notes: Heb “was found in it”; the referent (the city) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “he delivered.” The verb וּמִלַּט (umillat, from מָלַט, malat, “to deliver”) is functioning either in an indicative sense (past definite action: “he delivered”) or in a modal sense (past potential: “he could have delivered”). The literal meaning of זָכַר (zakhar, “to remember”) in the following line harmonizes with the indicative: “but no one remembered that poor man [afterward].” However, the modal is supported by v. 16: “A poor man’s wisdom is despised; no one ever listens to his advice.” This approach must nuance זָכַר (“to remember”) as “[no one] listened to [that poor man].” Most translations favor the indicative approach: “he delivered” or “he saved” (KJV, RSV, NRSV, NAB, ASV, NASB, MLB, NIV); however, some adopt the modal nuance: “he might have saved” (NEB, NJPS, NASB margin).
Heb “remembered.”

verses.zh: 我就说，智慧胜过勇力；然而那贫穷人的智慧被人藐视，他的话也无人听从。
verses.en: So I concluded that wisdom is better than might,[NOTE:1] but a poor man’s wisdom is despised; no one ever listens[NOTE:2] to his advice.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “power.”
The participle form נִשְׁמָעִים (nishmaʿim, Niphal participle masculine plural from שָׁמַע, [shamaʿ] “to listen”) is used verbally to emphasize a continual, durative, gnomic action.
Heb “his words are never listened to.”

verses.zh: 宁可在安静之中听智慧人的言语，不听掌管愚昧人的喊声。
verses.en: The words of the wise are heard in quiet,more than the shouting of a ruler is heard[NOTE:1] among fools.
notes: The phrase “is heard” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity and smoothness. Note its appearance in the previous line.
verses.commentary: 9:17-18 Wisdom has a place in life. It is "better" than. . . ., but it brings no lasting advantage/profit.

verses.zh: 智慧胜过打仗的兵器；但一个罪人能败坏许多善事。
verses.en: Wisdom is better than weapons of war,but one sinner can destroy much that is good.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible
for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the
Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject
divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the
original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.
